draft.title: Rollback plans are not the real control
draft.body:
Rollback plans sound tidy until you look at the actual workflow risk. In a small business, the problem is usually not “can we undo it later?” It is “what happens while this automation is running?” If the wrong customer reply goes out, a duplicate invoice is created, or a manual step gets bypassed, rolling back after the fact does not erase the damage already in motion.

That is why rollback is not enough on its own. It protects the previous state. It does not stop bad data, bad answers, or bad decisions from propagating. For an owner, the better question is simple: which part of this process needs a gate before anything is committed?

Start small and manual. Pick one repeatable workflow you are considering automating. Write down the three most damaging failure modes: wrong data, missed items, and duplicates. Then choose one human approval step that would block the worst one before it reaches payment, the inbox, or the CRM. If you are testing invoice extraction, for example, you can spot-check a few entries against the source documents before anything is posted. That is a control. A rollback plan is still useful, but it is the backup plan, not the main defense.

Bareni’s standard setup keeps accounts in the customer’s name and hands over finished code, but that is policy and no-lock-in positioning, not a warranty. The practical move is still the same: control the workflow first, then decide whether automation belongs there at all.

- RAG means retrieving relevant approved company documents before answering; in
  plain terms, the assistant looks in company material rather than the open web.
- Never imply production operation, customer validation, real customer documents,
  billing, rate limiting, or proven scale.

### Accounts-payable automation

- Self-built demo using entirely synthetic data for a fictional German
  manufacturer. Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
- Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
  refusal of agent approval/payment attempts, and persistent audit records work.
  The blocked payment demonstration is a manual trigger and simulated, not a real
  transfer. Three-way matching against purchase orders and receipts is not built.
- Never claim actual payment, customer deployment, observed customer results,
  working OCR/PDF ingestion, or working three-way matching. EUR 473k belongs to an
  old synthetic calculation model and must not be used as a customer result.

### Atlas Partner

- Self-built prototype, not a mock-up and not a finished SaaS product. Root-page
  website analysis and ICP creation work. Some prospecting works but depends on an
  older LinkedIn-search vendor and has encountered usage limits; employee-count
  filtering exists only in the UI. The seven-stage pipeline works through a
  dropdown, not drag-and-drop. Delegated Cal.com booking can add a booking to the
  pipeline.
- Direct Google Calendar/Meet integration, complete inbound form capture, billing,
  self-service, and multi-customer operation do not exist. Do not call it a customer
  case study or a finished product.

## Scope boundaries

- Bareni currently declines high-sensitivity medical, legal, and financial work;
  bulk cold-email automation; scan-heavy OCR-dependent workflows; and requests
  that require unsupported compliance or security guarantees. Present these as
  current scope discipline, not claims that the work can never be automated.
- Do not say cold email is always illegal in Germany and do not give legal advice.
- Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

## Voice, claims, numbers, and calls to action

- Sound like a technical expert using plain language: direct, calm, practical,
  founder-to-founder, and trustworthy. "The build stays technical; the conversation
  doesn't." Explain necessary jargon immediately.
- Trust outranks friendliness. At most one restrained dry-humour or understatement
  sentence per post. No memes, exclamation-mark bursts, hype, or jokes for their own
  sake.
- Never use revolutionary, 10x, game-changing, cutting-edge, unleash, supercharge,
  magic, or equivalent hype. Prefer concrete mechanisms and measured outcomes.
- Numbers require a source and status. Keep observed results, estimates, targets,
  synthetic data, and examples distinct. Never invent a benchmark, guarantee, ROI,
  saving, revenue lift, productivity result, or thesis-validated capability.
- Allowed: "we built" the three self-built demos/prototype; description of the
  actual features and disclosed limits; and description of Bareni as a consulting
  practice being built by the thesis author.
- Do not use a founder name, face, or career history as authority. Do not imply a
  multi-person team, legal registration, or current customer relationships.
- Standard primary CTA: "Book a free 30-minute diagnostic". Use it only for
  purchase-intent content, once, at the end. Informational posts use no CTA or one
  soft closing sentence. Demo CTA: "Watch the demo". At most one primary and one
  secondary CTA, only at the end. No popups, repeated CTAs, fabricated scarcity,
  countdowns, or pressure. A factual capacity statement such as "We take on a small
  number of pilots at a time" is allowed when relevant.

task_evidence.text:
Owner-authorized task instructions (not evidence of business outcomes): FROZEN PERSONA
# Frozen Marketing persona profile

- Audience: the English-speaking owner-operator of a 1-10-person small business who has
  tried ChatGPT but has not integrated AI into a real workflow.
- Decision context: the owner compares a bounded automation investment with continuing
  manual work or hiring; final approval and business authority remain human.
- Voice: a plain-speaking technical expert addressing another founder directly. Trust and
  operational specificity take priority over enthusiasm.
- Evidence boundary: never imply customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, revenue lift,
  production readiness, or capabilities beyond the supplied evidence.
- Practicality: explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step. Do not force AI where it is unsuitable.
- Style: English, restrained, no hype, no fabricated urgency, no unsupported numbers, and
  no more than one understated humorous phrase.
- CTA: use none unless the task explicitly authorises one. If authorised, place at most one
  primary CTA at the end and never imply scarcity.
- Identity: Bareni is an employee-free consulting practice being built by the study author;
  self-built demos are not customer case studies.


APPROVED TASK
**Audience:** CEO of a 1-10-person small business.
**Owner-specified abstract topic:** why rollback plans are not enough
**Task:** Turn the abstract topic into a bounded Bareni workflow decision. Explain one practical next step.
**Format pattern:** CF-05.
**Persona focus:** PF-01_problem_awareness.
**Evidence boundary:** Use only approved Bareni evidence. Do not invent customers, deployments, outcomes, savings, capabilities, or a multi-person team.
**CTA rule:** None.
**Output:** English LinkedIn post; body target 1200-1500 characters, hard range 150-2000; title stored separately.

constraints.text: No invented customer, deployment, result, number, capability, multi-person team, or sales CTA.
No autonomous money movement or high-risk decision; no excluded service.
Preserve the frozen persona, approved evidence status, and human approval boundaries.
Use plain English; keep examples or proposals distinct from existing capabilities or observed results.

selected_lessons.application: The task explicitly rules out CTA; L01 confirms that no diagnostic booking invitation, meeting prompt, or indirect engagement offer should appear. End with a neutral next-step observation instead.
C02 describes customer-owned accounts and no lock-in as policy positioning, not legal warranty. Preserve this qualifier if rollback or contingency language touches retention or exit.

The abstract topic 'why rollback plans are not enough' requires grounding in a concrete workflow decision within Bareni's scope. Where the evidence does not support a general business principle, replace it with a specific diagnostic question or control decision the owner can make.

steps.instruction: Reframe 'rollback plans' from disaster-recovery jargon into the owner's actual risk: a workflow automation that fails mid-execution, leaving manual work stranded. Identify the one repeatable business process the owner is considering automating (e.g., invoice data entry, customer-inquiry routing), and name the visible failure mode: system down, wrong data passed forward, or human step bypassed.

Explain that rollback alone is insufficient because it returns you to manual work but does not prevent the damage already caused (wrong customer answers sent, duplicate payments, missed leads). A rollback plan protects past state; a control plan prevents bad outcomes from propagating. The owner's real question is not 'Can we undo this?' but 'What stops this breaking my business while it runs?'

Describe one concrete control that applies to the owner's workflow without building the full automation yet. Example: if automating invoice extraction, run the LLM on a test batch, spot-check three extractions against source PDFs, and set an approval threshold (amounts over USD 5000 require human sign-off before posting). This is not a rollback; it is a gate that runs before commitment.

Clarify Bareni's approach: accounts and tools stay in your name, and finished code is yours to keep. This means you own the decision to pause, modify, or roll back the automation itself—not just the data. Frame this as operational autonomy and standard practice, not a legal warranty.

Give the owner one practical next step: before building, identify the single repeatable workflow causing the most friction or error. Write down the three most damaging failure modes (wrong data, missed items, duplicates). Then ask: which failure would a human approval step before commitment prevent? Use that answer to sketch the minimal control needed, not the perfect system.

Close with a neutral observation: 'Rollback plans answer the wrong question for automation in a small business. The right question is what stops a mistake from cascading before it happens. Start with controls, not contingency plans.'

constraints_to_preserve.handling: No invented customer deployments, observed results, savings, or sales CTA. All examples use synthetic or hypothetical workflow scenarios (e.g., invoice extraction test batch) as illustrations, not proof of capability.
P04 confirms human approval is mandatory before money movement (e.g., payments); P03 includes approval gates as a control, not autonomous execution.
All steps use the frozen persona voice: plain-speaking, founder-to-founder, operationally specific, and restrained. No hype, no urgency language, no multi-person team claims.
Examples (invoice test batch, USD 5000 threshold) are illustrative proposals and remain distinct from Bareni's built systems (C03). L02 applied to preserve policy language around customer ownership.

evidence.quote: The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI fits
have a frequent, repeatable workflow with a measurable outcome

explain one observable workflow decision, threshold, diagnostic question,
  control, or next step

ledger.rationale: This is an instruction to reframe the topic and pose a diagnostic identification step, not an assertion of current implementation or observed customer behaviour. Identifying the one recurring workflow is consistent with the approved diagnostic scope.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as a proposed reframing and diagnostic prompt for the reader. Use generic workflow examples (invoice data entry, inquiry routing) as illustrations only; do not attribute them to any customer, deployment or observed failure event.

evidence.quote: Arithmetic checks, duplicate-invoice blocking, amount-based human-only approval,
Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

ledger.rationale: The claim advances a reasoning line and a question the owner should ask rather than reporting an observed outcome; the underlying control logic (prevention gates, duplicate blocking, human approval) is consistent with approved evidence.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as explanatory argument and diagnostic question. Present damage examples (wrong answers, duplicate payments, missed leads) as generic risk categories, not as incidents that occurred at Bareni or any customer; do not imply measured losses.

evidence.quote:
Text-based LLM invoice extraction was verified, while the default
  demo uses pre-extracted files. PDF/scan ingestion and OCR are not implemented.
Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

ledger.rationale: This proposes a control the reader could apply and an illustrative threshold; it does not assert an existing Bareni capability. Note that the suggested spot-check against source PDFs must not imply Bareni has working PDF/scan ingestion or OCR, which approved evidence states are not implemented.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep explicitly as a proposed pre-build control with the reader doing the checking manually. Mark the USD 5000 figure as an illustrative example threshold the owner sets, not a Bareni benchmark or default, and avoid wording that suggests automated PDF/OCR extraction exists.

evidence.quote:
Finished code is handed to the customer. Database, automation-tool, and API
  accounts are in the customer's name from the start.
Describe this as policy and no-lock-in positioning, not an absolute legal warranty.

ledger.rationale: The account-ownership and code-handover core is supported, and the claim already asks for framing as standard practice rather than warranty. However the inference that the customer therefore 'owns the decision to pause, modify, or roll back the automation itself' is an added conclusion not stated in evidence and needs limiting to what the ownership arrangement actually covers.
ledger.use_guidance: Add the qualification that this is Bareni's stated policy and no-lock-in positioning, and confine the statement to account ownership and code handover; do not extend it into a guarantee of technical rollback capability or an absolute legal warranty.

evidence.quote:
The diagnostic identifies the one recurring workflow, says honestly whether AI
  fits
Human approval is mandatory for money movement and other high-risk decisions.

ledger.rationale: A manual next step the owner performs before any build; it asserts no implementation, outcome or capability, and the human-approval framing matches approved constraints.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as the single practical next step, entirely manual and reader-performed. Do not attach expected time savings, error-rate reductions or any numeric benefit, and do not turn it into an invitation to contact Bareni.

evidence.quote: Informational posts use no CTA or one soft closing sentence.

ledger.rationale: This is an instruction for a neutral closing observation rather than a factual assertion about Bareni or the market; it complies with the no-CTA rule for this task.
ledger.use_guidance: Keep as a neutral closing observation with no meeting prompt, diagnostic offer or conversation invitation. Keep the tone restrained and free of hype terms.

selected_lessons.text: For informational marketing content, treat any invitation to book a diagnostic, discuss the situation, or continue the conversation as a CTA unless the task explicitly authorises one. This includes indirect meeting prompts and direct brand-level offers such as a free 30-minute diagnostic. End with a neutral practical observation or next-step note instead of a meeting prompt.
When approved evidence presents an operational practice as policy or positioning, keep that qualifier in the copy. Do not rewrite it as an absolute guarantee or warranty-level statement.
If the source set does not support a substantive explanatory claim, replace it with a neutral workflow prompt or decision step rather than filling the gap with general background explanation.
